item.text:
1. **Section 2(1) — “Artificial intelligence model” and “artificial intelligence system” are undefined.** Companies could argue that a product is an algorithm, agent, service, ensemble, or software platform rather than a covered “model” or “system,” and the inconsistent use of the two terms creates uncertainty about what is regulated.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — The compute threshold is underinclusive.** A system capable of superintelligent performance could be trained below \(10^{26}\) operations through algorithmic improvements, transfer learning, pretrained components, synthetic data, or other efficiency gains unless and until the Secretary separately designates it under paragraph (B).

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — Exactly \(10^{26}\) operations is permitted.** The phrase “greater than” excludes a training run using precisely the threshold amount.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Computing power” is incorrectly equated with a number of operations.** Computing power ordinarily describes a rate or capacity, while the provision measures cumulative computation, creating a technical ambiguity that defendants could exploit.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Integer or floating-point operations” lacks a counting methodology.** The bill does not specify precision, sparsity treatment, skipped operations, specialized operations, estimated versus actual operations, or whether data processing, architecture search, simulation, and post-training computation count.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Single training run” is undefined and easily circumvented.** A developer could divide work among sequential runs, checkpoints, fine-tuning stages, cooperating entities, or distributed and federated training jobs, each nominally below the threshold.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — Post-training and inference scaling may escape the threshold.** The definition does not clearly aggregate reinforcement learning, fine-tuning, tool use, test-time computation, memory, retrieval, or inference-time search with the original training run.

8. **Section 2(1)(A) — Reused components are not addressed.** A company could assemble or fine-tune multiple sub-threshold models or imported pretrained components while arguing that no single model was trained above the threshold.

9. **Section 2(1)(A) — The numerical threshold cannot be updated.** There is no adjustment mechanism for changes in hardware, algorithms, measurement practices, or evidence about dangerous capabilities.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — The responsible “Secretary” is never identified.** The bill refers elsewhere to both Commerce and State, so it is unclear which Secretary makes coverage determinations.

11. **Section 2(1)(B) — The capability standard is highly vague.** “Substantially exceeding,” “human performance,” “most,” and “cognitive tasks” lack benchmarks, comparison populations, testing conditions, or a defined universe of tasks, inviting evasion and due-process challenges.

12. **Section 2(1)(B) — Coverage depends on an affirmative government determination.** A highly capable system may remain lawful until the Secretary acts, allowing development or deployment during agency delay and creating disputes about whether a later determination applies to earlier conduct.

13. **Section 2(1)(B) — No designation procedure is provided.** There are no requirements for testing, evidence, notice, publication, hearings, emergency determinations, effective dates, reconsideration, or judicial review.

14. **Section 2(1)(B) — The delegation lacks meaningful standards.** The broad and undefined discretion given to the Secretary creates both inconsistent-enforcement risk and a possible nondelegation or arbitrary-and-capricious challenge.

15. **Section 2(2) — “U.S. person” omits major categories.** It does not expressly include permanent residents, U.S. nationals, partnerships, LLCs, nonprofits, trusts, associations, governmental entities, or other non-corporate organizations.

16. **Section 2(2) — Foreign subsidiaries and controlled entities are excluded.** A U.S. company could conduct the work abroad through a separately incorporated foreign subsidiary, joint venture, contractor, or shell company not itself organized under state law.

17. **Section 2(2) — Corporate coverage is territorially incomplete.** Corporations organized under federal, territorial, tribal, or District of Columbia law may contest coverage because the definition expressly says “under the laws of a State.”

18. **Section 2(3) — “Data center,” “operator,” and “advanced AI chips” are undefined.** These omissions permit disputes over colocation facilities, cloud providers, leased equipment, specialized accelerators, and which party has the registration duty.

19. **Section 2(3) — The chip threshold is readily avoided.** Facilities with exactly 50,000 chips are excluded, and companies can distribute chips among adjacent buildings, campuses, subsidiaries, or nominally separate facilities.

20. **Section 2(3) — “Containing” is ambiguous.** It is unclear whether chips in storage, disconnected chips, customer-owned chips, leased chips, or chips temporarily present at a facility count.

21. **Section 3(a) — Core prohibited acts are undefined.** “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” do not establish when conduct begins or ends and may not clearly cover continued operation, updates, fine-tuning, integration, or providing access through an API.

22. **Section 3(a) — Important enabling conduct is not prohibited.** The section does not expressly cover possession, acquisition, import, export, sale, licensing, financing, hosting, chip provision, publication of weights, assistance, attempted violations, or civil aiding and abetting.

23. **Section 3(a) — Territorial language is uncertain.** “In the United States” does not clearly resolve remote activity, cross-border cloud services, training spread across jurisdictions, or foreign actors directing activity into the United States.

24. **Section 3(a) — Offshore evasion remains possible.** Foreign persons may develop prohibited systems abroad and serve U.S. customers from abroad, while U.S. persons may participate through foreign-controlled intermediaries unless their own conduct can be proved.

25. **Section 3(b) — The grandfather clause is extremely broad and permanent.** Any covered system whose “training began” before enactment appears exempt from every prohibition, including later development and deployment, with no deadline, capability ceiling, or safety conditions.

26. **Section 3(b) — “Training began” is undefined and gameable.** A company could perform a token initialization or preliminary training step before enactment and claim that a much later, materially different training effort is grandfathered.

27. **Section 3(b) — Derivatives and modifications are unresolved.** The bill does not say when retraining, fine-tuning, architectural changes, new checkpoints, copies, or successor versions become new systems rather than exempt existing systems.

28. **Section 3(c) — The safety-evaluation exception can swallow the prohibition.** It is based only on an asserted “purpose,” with no preapproval, independent supervision, scale limit, security rules, reporting, or requirement that safety be the sole or primary purpose.

29. **Section 3(c) — The exception permits the dangerous acts themselves.** Because it exempts “activities” from all of subsection (a), a company could train, develop, or deploy a covered system while characterizing the activity as a safety evaluation.

30. **Section 4(a) — Registration has no deadline or implementing procedure.** The bill does not say when an existing or newly covered facility must register, what information registration must contain, or when changes must be reported.

31. **Section 4 — The registry reaches only very large facilities.** Dangerous workloads conducted across multiple smaller facilities, on foreign infrastructure, or through distributed cloud capacity would trigger no registration or reporting duty.

32. **Section 4(b) — Reporting requirements are too vague.** “Describing the computing workloads” establishes no required data fields, granularity, retention period, measurement method, or duty to identify customers, models, compute totals, or linked workloads at other facilities.

33. **Section 4(b) — Self-certification is weak and undefined.** It does not specify who must certify, the certification standard, personal accountability, supporting records, or consequences for a false or incomplete certification.

34. **Sections 4 and 5 — Registry violations have no penalty.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3, leaving failure to register, failure to report, and false or late reports without an express civil or criminal consequence.

35. **Sections 3–5 — No enforcement authority is assigned.** No agency is expressly authorized to investigate, inspect facilities, audit compute records, issue subpoenas, compel evaluations, promulgate rules, seek injunctions, or bring civil actions.

36. **Section 5(a) — Civil enforcement mechanics are missing.** The bill does not identify who assesses or recovers the penalty, what procedure applies, the limitations period, available defenses, or which court has jurisdiction.

37. **Section 5(a) — The per-day unit is ambiguous.** It is unclear whether penalties apply per system, actor, training run, prohibited act, or corporate group, potentially limiting major violators to a single $1 million daily penalty.

38. **Section 5(a) — The maximum penalty may be merely a cost of doing business.** There is no minimum penalty, disgorgement, forfeiture, destruction requirement, license consequence, or penalty tied to revenue, compute expenditure, or economic benefit.

39. **Section 5(b) — “Willfully” creates a demanding criminal proof requirement.** Defendants may argue that the government must prove knowledge that their conduct violated this particular statute, especially given the bill’s vague technical terms and discretionary designation process.

40. **Section 5(b) — Individual responsibility is unclear.** The bill does not expressly establish liability for responsible executives or officials who direct, authorize, or knowingly fail to prevent corporate violations.

41. **Sections 5 and 8 — The penalty and effective-date provisions conflict.** Section 5 covers violations “on or after” enactment, but section 8 says the Act takes effect 180 days later, creating uncertainty and potential retroactivity or fair-notice challenges.

42. **Section 6 — The international-negotiation duty is largely unenforceable.** “Shall seek to negotiate” requires neither a completed agreement nor specified diplomatic actions, and the 18-month language is ambiguous about whether negotiations merely must begin by then.

43. **Section 6 — “Equivalent” international prohibitions are undefined.** The provision sets no required verification, inspections, enforcement, compute controls, remedies, withdrawal rules, or standard for determining equivalence.

44. **Section 6 — No interim cross-border controls are provided.** The bill contains no chip, model-weight, technical-assistance, investment, or cloud-compute controls to prevent covered development from moving overseas while negotiations proceed.

45. **Section 7(a) — The National Academies process is incomplete.** No one is directed to request the report, and there is no deadline, required methodology, safety standard, evidentiary burden, or specification of what the report must conclude.

46. **Section 7(a) — “Can be developed safely” is undefined.** Congress could terminate the prohibition based on an unspecified degree or type of safety, without requiring proof that extinction risk has been eliminated or reduced to a defined level.

47. **Section 7 — The two termination mechanisms conflict in purpose.** Section 7(a) suggests the prohibition lasts until an affirmative safety finding, but section 7(b) terminates the entire Act after ten years even if no such finding is ever made.

48. **Section 7(b) — The unconditional sunset eliminates all safeguards.** Registration, reporting, penalties, and the prohibition all disappear after ten years, potentially while dangerous systems remain prohibited in principle and without any transition or renewal mechanism.

49. **Section 7(b) — Treatment of pending and accrued cases is unclear.** Saying the Act “shall cease to have effect” may generate litigation over ongoing injunctions, reporting obligations, investigations, and liability for pre-sunset conduct.

50. **Act-wide — There is no severability clause.** If a court invalidates a central provision—particularly the vague capability standard, delegation, or penalty scheme—litigants could argue that more or all of the Act must fall with it.

51. **Act-wide — No resources or implementation mandate are supplied.** The bill authorizes no appropriations, staffing, technical monitoring program, secure reporting system, or implementation timetable, making effective detection and enforcement doubtful.

52. **Act-wide — The bill lacks anti-evasion and aggregation rules.** Related persons, facilities, runs, models, and transactions are not aggregated, so regulated parties can restructure operations formally while continuing substantially the same activity.
